# EmulationStation native UI/UX practices

Survey of `ROCKNIX/emulationstation-next` (2026-07-24) for building native experiences
(cloud sync, backup/restore, issue #15 L2/L3). Source lives in the separate ES repo;
this file guides any work there.

**This file was split on 2026-09-12** (#147). Maintainer: *"let's split up the
native UI into parts."* The mechanics stayed here; the words a player reads
went to `es-player-text.md`, and the codebase's sharp edges to
`es-code-traps.md` (D-WORKFLOW-008).

## Where things live

- `es-app/src/guis/` — application pages (GuiMenu, GuiControllersSettings, GuiMoonlight,
  GuiBackupStart/GuiBackup, GuiBios, GuiFileBrowser, GuiBatoceraStore, ...).
- `es-core/src/guis/` — primitives: `GuiMsgBox` (1–3 button dialog), `GuiTextEditPopup` /
  `GuiTextEditPopupKeyboard` (on-screen keyboard), `GuiInfoPopup`, `GuiInputConfig`.
- `es-core/src/components/` — `MenuComponent`, `ComponentList`, `SwitchComponent`,
  `OptionListComponent`, `SliderComponent`, `ButtonComponent`, `BusyComponent`
  (spinner), `AsyncNotificationComponent` (the progress card: 0.9 of the screen
  width, centred at the top -- § Spacing; it read "top-right" here until T35's
  L-22 found the words stale against `Window.cpp:1192`, PL-23, 2026-11-01).

## The other files that carry the interface law

This file is the mechanics. Three sibling rules and two `docs/` documents carry
the rest; the two under `docs/` load nowhere, so open them when the work is
theirs -- the 2026-09-12 sweep (#147) found that no rule file named any of
them, which is how a page gets built against half the house style.

| File | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| `es-player-text.md` (rule) | every word a player reads: the four tiers and the two verbs, "back up" vs "backup", the serial comma, game save vs save state, Wi-Fi, how much text a row may carry, and the outcome vocabulary every run ends with |
| `es-ui-style-guide.md` (rule) | the seven row builders, the `multiLine` trap, `addSaveFunc` vs `setOnChangedCallback`, the reboot flags, the four gates in precedence order, button order and the back-button accelerator, confirmation registers, glyphs, placeholder words (`AUTO`, `NONE`, `<NOT SET>`), the three type sizes |
| `es-code-traps.md` (rule) | the sharp edges, each found by debugging: button-bar lifetimes, rclone's piped progress, xgettext and non-ASCII comments, help-bar prompts, `TextComponent`'s measuring, and where pure string code lives |
| `docs/es-menu-map.md` | where a row belongs: the two entry points, the `addGroup` sections that are the real IA, read-only facts before editable settings, destructive work behind ADVANCED, the kid/kiosk collapse, and cloud's one door |
| `docs/conflict-wizard-ia.md` | the wizard's architecture: what counts as a conflict, the header's count, nothing transfers until COMPLETE, the column and badge vocabulary |

**A row added, moved or renamed updates `docs/es-menu-map.md` in the same
change (D-UI-039, maintainer 2026-09-11).** The rule is stated in the map
itself, which is the one place somebody who has not opened it will not read
it; it is repeated here so it loads with the rest.

**And it is checked, because for a month it was not kept.** `tools/es-menu-map-check`
reads every screen title in the EmulationStation commit the package pins --
not a working tree, which is usually somebody's feature branch -- and fails on
one the map neither describes nor declares. On 2026-09-18 it found **30 of 51
screens** missing, six of them pages this fork wrote itself: FINISH RESTORE
SETUP's three password pages, and the setup wizard's WHICH CONNECTION?, SSH
PASSWORD and CLOUD SETUP COMPLETE. A documentation practice that nothing
verifies decays exactly like an unverified guard, and for the same reason --
nobody finds out.

A screen we deliberately do not map is declared in the map's **`## Not mapped`**
section as `- TITLE -- why`, which is where an upstream page we never touch
belongs. Two consequences worth knowing: adding a ROCKNIX row to one of those
pages means mapping it properly and deleting its declaration, and a declaration
naming a screen that no longer exists fails the check too -- it would otherwise
sit there excusing the next screen that reuses the name. The check runs in
`tools/vm-qa` as the `menumap` suite, beside `french`.

Two house rules from `es-ui-style-guide.md` are worth carrying at this altitude
because they decide safety, not looks:

- **YES first in a confirmation**, and the back-button accelerator binds to a
  button named exactly `NO` or `OK` -- otherwise it falls through to the last
  button, so back must never land on the destructive choice.
- **Dim, don't hide.** An unconfigured feature stays visible at alpha `0x50`
  and offers its setup, keeping its description. A *button*, by contrast, is
  gated by existence: a null callback means CONTINUE does not exist until it
  would work.

## Core patterns (use these, don't invent)

- **Settings page**: `new GuiSettings(window, _("TITLE"))` + `addGroup` / `addEntry`
  (action rows) / `addWithLabel` (switch/option rows) / `addSaveFunc` (apply-on-close);
  `s->setVariable("reboot", true)` + finalize for reboot-needed changes.
- **Text/credential input**: `GuiSettings::addInputTextConfigRow(title, settingsID,
  password, storeInSettings)` — binds a row to SystemConf (default) or Settings
  (`storeInSettings=true`), opens the on-screen keyboard, masks with `password=true`.
  This is the tool for wifi/RetroAchievements/ScreenScraper credential re-entry
  (`"wifi.key"`, `"global.retroachievements.password"`, `ScreenScraperPass`).
- **Confirmation**: `GuiMsgBox(window, _("TEXT"), _("YES"), cb, _("NO"), nullptr)`.
  Dialog text MUST describe actual behavior (see the backuptool drift lesson).
- **Toast**: `window->displayNotificationMessage(_("..."), ms)`.
- **Background job with progress card, for fast work only (D-UI-078)**: `window->createAsyncNotificationComponent()`
  -- two rows (title, text) by default; pass `true` for the third, the action
  row, when the outcome carries a recovery clause. The cloud card composed one
  for a day and had no row to draw it on (blindspot 35).
  + worker thread updating it — see `ThreadedBluetooth.cpp` (also used by content
  installers). Seconds, not minutes: anything longer is the fourth tier below.
- **Busy spinner while loading**: `GuiLoading<T>` (async worker + result callback), or a
  full-screen `GuiComponent` owning a `BusyComponent` + small state machine — see
  `GuiBackup.cpp` (batocera's native user-data backup).
- **Run an OS command**: `Utils::Platform::runSystemCommand(cmd, name, window)` runs `cmd`
  through `/usr/bin/sh -c` and blocks the calling thread until it exits (an interrupted
  `waitpid` is not retried); it reads neither `name` nor `window`, so nothing is shown while
  it runs, and it returns 0 whatever the command did (`Platform.cpp:853-880` at the pin
  `16dbac5211`, T36 L-13). A call on the interface thread freezes the screen for the
  command's whole run (#1220); a caller that needs the outcome reads it another way.
  `/usr/bin/run "<cmd>"` for fullscreen console TUIs (current parity flows). Native pages
  should prefer headless backends + the async patterns above over console hops.
- **A file another process writes is read uncached.** `Utils::FileSystem::exists`
  remembers a miss while `UseFileCache` is on (the default) until a game launch
  or a restart clears the cache, so a stamp the scripts write, or the
  `rclone.conf` the wizard makes, reads as absent for the rest of the session
  on any page that asked before it existed. Pass `exists(path, false)` for
  those (the cloud rows read NOT DONE ON THIS DEVICE YET after a run had
  stamped, 2026-09-10).
- **Gating**: `ApiSystem::isScriptingSupported(ApiSystem::FEATURE)` for capability-based
  entries (batocera-style backends); plain `Utils::FileSystem::exists("/usr/bin/tool")`
  for OS-shipped scripts (our cloud entries). Respect `isFullUI`/kid-mode branches.
- **OS event hooks**: `Scripting::fireEvent("game-start"/"game-end"/...)` executes
  scripts from user ES `scripts/<event>/`, the ES exe dir (`/usr/bin/scripts/<event>/`,
  read-only image — our game-end hook), and `/var/run/emulationstation/scripts/<event>/`.

## Tabbed pages: the strip is a focus stop

`MenuComponent(window, title, tabbedUI = true)` puts a `ComponentTab` strip
above the rows. Since #65 (2026-09-05, D-UI-021) the strip is a focusable grid
cell: up from the first row lands on it, left/right there switch tabs, down
returns to the rows, and the wrap runs strip → rows → buttons → strip. A page
opens on its first row. Rows keep left/right for themselves, which is how an
option row cycles in place everywhere else in ES.

It was wired the other way for years — the strip non-focusable, and
`MenuComponent::input` handing every left/right on the page to it — so the 23
option rows on SCRAPER → OPTIONS could only be changed through the A-button
popup, and the focused rendering `ComponentTab` had always carried (a full
selector bar over the active tab) was never once drawn. **Do not route a
direction key to one component from everywhere on a page.** Give the
component a focus stop and let the grid deliver the key to whatever holds the
focus; a component that needs a key from anywhere is a component in the wrong
place.

Four screens still route left/right to their strips themselves
(`GuiThemeInstaller`, `GuiBatoceraStore`, `GuiKeyMappingEditor`,
`GuiKeyboardtopads`). They move to the same model with #63.

## The cards at the link's return: saves first, then one batch (D-UI-101, D-UI-109)

When the link returns with an exit sync owed, awards to send and a top-up
due, the player sees SYNCING SAVES TO THE CLOUD first, and then the
RetroAchievements cards together: the send card, and the top-up's card
stacked under it. `ProxyCards::linkReturned` starts the owed sync when
there is one and marks the batch owed; `afterSync`, called as every
automatic sync card ends, runs the batch then -- the send probe and the
top-up -- and with no saves owed the batch runs at once. The send card
takes the proxy's flush stamp itself, waiting up to ten seconds for it
once the queue is empty, so the probe at a later sync card's end does not
report the same batch again. Two rounds got here: before #298 the send's
end started the saves and the top-up's outcome landed after them
(*"they should be batched"*); #298 put the saves after both, and on the
device the proxy's stamp, written four seconds after its queue emptied,
was found by the probe at the saves card's end and shown as a second send
card -- RetroAchievements, saves, RetroAchievements (#305, the maintainer:
*"sync saves first (which makes sense), and then it would do the
RetroAchievements following that"*).

**And the top-up is two things (D-RA-035, D-UI-103).** At the link's return the
control script asks one question -- was a game played since the last attempt
(RetroArch's history newer than the mark)? -- and runs the recently played
pass alone when yes, with its card (RETROACHIEVEMENTS (OFFLINE) over
`GETTING GAME N OF M READY...`, D-UI-107),
or exits before the probe when no. New games are the index's: the hasher at
startup and after UPDATE GAMELISTS, which ends in the full top-up with its
card stacked under the game list update's. So a wake after a night shows
nothing and costs a moment (the maintainer met a nine-second card there,
#299), and the card, when it shows, is a run with something to look for.

## Spacing (house style)

Values live in one place each, so a screen never makes its own decision.

- **Buttons on a menu's button bar**: `BUTTON_GRID_HORIZ_PADDING` in
  `es-core/src/components/MenuComponent.cpp`, **0.022 of screen width**
  (14px on a 640px handheld panel). Every ES screen ends in this bar, so
  changing it here is the whole style rule.

  It was `0.0052` — 3px on a handheld — which reads as one control rather
  than two, and puts a destructive choice a thumb's width from a safe one.
  Two adjacent buttons must be separated far enough that hitting the wrong
  one is a decision, not a slip.

- **Rows on a cloud-setup page**: `CLOUD_SETUP_ROW_PADDING` in `GuiMenu.cpp`.

- **How wide and where a progress card sits**: 0.9 of screen width, centred
  at the top — `AsyncNotificationComponent`'s constructor for the size,
  `Window::renderAsyncNotifications` for the position (the latter re-applies
  it every frame, so both must agree). 0.9 is `GuiInfoPopup`'s cap and the
  widest this app lets a non-blocking overlay get. Past half the screen a
  card pinned to a corner reads as a panel that failed to fit rather than a
  placement anybody chose, so anything wider than that is centred.

  The four **surface** tiers, so a new surface picks the right one (not
  the four data tiers of `es-player-text.md` § Conventions -- settings,
  saves, ROMs and BIOS, game content -- which are a different list that
  happens to be the same length):

  | Surface | Width | Position | Blocks input | Ends |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | `Splash` (boot, gamelist reload, launch) | full screen; its bar is 0.5W | whole screen | yes | when the work does |
  | `GuiInfoPopup` (toast) | fits text, capped 0.9W | top, centred | no | on a timer |
  | `AsyncNotificationComponent` (progress) | 0.9W | top, centred | no | when the work does |
  | `GuiCloudTransfer`, `GuiOfflineScan` (long job) | full screen | whole screen | yes; CANCEL is the one way out while it runs (D-UI-078) | **when dismissed** |

  Full-*screen* is a modal takeover, not a wider card — do not reach for it
  for work the player can keep playing through.

  **One floating surface at a time (D-UI-093, 2026-09-25).** The toast and
  the card sit in the same place, and on the RG35XX SP the OFFLINE
  ACHIEVEMENTS HAVE BEEN SENT toast drew over the saves sync's card.
  Maintainer: *"it's confusing to have a pop-up over a pop-up. That should
  be something we always avoid."* So `Window` shows them in turn: a queued
  toast is not started while a card is up, and a card created while a
  toast is up stops the toast and puts its words back on the queue, so
  they show after the card. Nothing is dropped; the order is the order
  things happened. A surface that must be seen at once is the fourth
  tier's page, not a second card.

  **A fourth-tier page is sat in, with CANCEL (D-UI-078, 2026-09-21).** A
  job measured in minutes gets a page that owns the screen until the job
  ends, and the only way out while it runs is CANCEL: a confirmation that
  says what cancelling means for that job -- start over, or resume where the
  job supports it -- then the stop. Every other press is refused, because
  there is nothing to choose. Backgrounding is for fast work only: the
  two-second save sync at startup and exit, a Bluetooth scan. Maintainer, on
  the RG35XX SP at the scan page's PRESS B TO KEEP SCANNING IN THE
  BACKGROUND: *"we should only allow things to run in the background when
  they're fast. If it's something that's going to take longer time, like
  scraping or doing the RetroAchievements offline work, we should force that
  to be on a foreground page."*

  It was the other way for a week. Audit #186 PL-07 made the scan page
  leaveable (B closed it, `OfflineScanJob` ran on, the SCAN GAMES row carried
  the live line, pressing the row reopened the page), and #187 gave
  `GuiCloudTransfer` the same shape in RC-11 (D-UI-060, D-UI-070). What that
  bought was every edge case of a job nobody is watching: no end signal, an
  outcome on a row the player has to go and find, a second press that has to
  know whether to reopen or refuse, a run that outlives the interface. The
  maintainer met the B prompt on the device, asked what would happen, and
  the honest answer was "nothing tells you" -- which is the whole case. A
  page that holds the player for the job's length is the simpler contract,
  and CANCEL is the way to give it back. The tell that a page has this wrong
  is a footer offering to leave it running. #241 carried the change, the
  scraper included. The other upstream cards -- the game index, the
  content installer, the OS update, the Bluetooth scan -- stay as they
  are (D-UI-079): the rule is for the lanes the fork works in, and an
  upstream surface outside them is not changed on the strength of it.

  **Anything automatic that moves data over the network is shown while it
  runs, and a launch over it asks (D-UI-095, 2026-09-26).** Maintainer:
  *"if there's activity happening in the background around
  RetroAchievements or save management, etc., we want to make sure we're
  showing the user what's going on. We want to enact the right gates to
  keep the user from proceeding without knowing what's going on."* So the
  startup and exit syncs, the proxy's send of held awards and the ctl's
  top-up each have a card in the third tier while they run, each stamps
  what it said (`last-sync-<origin>`), and `FileData::launchGame` asks the
  same shape of question over each -- the statement, one consequence, two
  verbs with the safe one last (`es-player-text.md` § Conventions,
  D-UI-096). A job the interface cannot stop (the proxy's own send) asks
  PLAY NOW / KEEP WAITING; one it can asks STOP IT AND PLAY / KEEP WAITING.
  Bookkeeping that reads the device and touches no network (the captures)
  stays silent. `ProxyCards` is the unit for the proxy's two jobs; the
  cards are one at a time (D-UI-093), the send card waiting for a sync
  card and an automatic sync that reached the network asking for it as it
  ends.

  **Duration decides between the last two, and the deciding column is
  "Ends".** A card is right for work somebody watches finish — a scrape, a
  hash, a two-second save sync. It is wrong for anything long enough to walk
  away from, because it closes itself the moment the job ends: a 1.4 GiB
  restore left nothing behind but a log file, and the player had to ask
  somebody else whether it had worked (2026-09-03).

  So a job measured in minutes gets a page that outlives it. Show the live
  line, a bar only where a real percentage exists behind it, elapsed time, and
  then the outcome — and refuse input while it runs, because there is nothing
  to choose and a stray press should not dismiss a page somebody is waiting
  on. `GuiCloudTransfer` follows `GuiBackup`'s shape (GuiComponent +
  BusyComponent + worker thread), which is this codebase's existing answer to
  a long job with a page of its own.

- **How solid a floating card is**: `NOTIFICATION_OPACITY` in
  `es-core/src/components/AsyncNotificationComponent.cpp`, **255**. Every
  themed surface in the app — menus, dialogs, `GuiInfoPopup` after its
  fade-in — draws its background at full opacity and lets the theme decide
  how solid to be. This card was the one exception at 200, and over the
  shipped theme's `0x111111` panel that let a fifth of the game art through:
  a progress line on a mid-grey smear that shifted with the box art behind
  it. The corners of `frame.png` fade to nothing regardless, so a card at
  full opacity still reads as an overlay rather than a page.

Screen-relative fractions, never pixel constants: these panels run from
640×480 to 1920×1080 and a fixed value is right on exactly one of them.

## Images in a menu row are themed as text unless you stop it

`ComponentList::render` calls `setColor(menuTheme->Text.color)` on **every
element of every row, every frame**, and `ImageComponent::setColor` is
`setColorShift`. So an image added to a row is tinted with the menu's muted
text colour continuously, and setting the shift once at construction does
nothing at all.

Text beside it in the same row keeps its own colour only when it sits inside
a `ComponentGrid`, whose `setColor` does not reach the labels within — which
is why a QR code looked dimmer than the address next to it.

Where an image must keep its own colours — a QR a phone camera has to read,
a logo, a screenshot — subclass and refuse the tint:

```cpp
class UntintedImageComponent : public ImageComponent {
public:
    void setColor(unsigned int) override { ImageComponent::setColorShift(0xFFFFFFFF); }
};
```

## A layout must not be computed from what it last produced

`MultiLineMenuEntry::layoutRows` sized its two rows from `mText->getSize()`
and `mSubstring->getSize()` -- which, after the first pass, are the cells
the grid handed those texts (0.9 and 1.1 of their natural heights), because
`TextComponent` stops sizing itself once it has been given a height. So
every `setDescription` moved the split by ten percent: a row refreshed
once looked a little tight, and the SCAN GAMES row, refreshed for each
game of a 37-game scan under the scan page, came back a screen tall with
the two texts drawn on top of each other (2026-09-22, #241; fixed in ES
`7c7ffab43` by measuring from the fonts). It had shipped in two candidates
because every walk scanned a handful of games (blindspot 44).

So a layout pass reads its inputs from something the pass does not write
-- the font, the text, the parent's width -- never from the sizes it set
last time. And a row that is refreshed on a timer is proved with a refresh
count in the hundreds, not with one.

## Code conventions

The language conventions that shared this heading -- the four tiers, the two
verbs, the serial comma, Wi-Fi, game save vs save state -- are
`es-player-text.md` § Conventions since the 2026-09-12 split, which is where a
citation of "`es-native-ui.md` § Conventions" resolves.

- Theme-aware colors/fonts via `ThemeData::getMenuTheme()`.
- Pages provide `getHelpPrompts()` so the bottom help bar stays accurate.
- **`GuiSettings::addSwitch(title, description, settingsID, bool, onChanged)` — the bool
  is `storeInSettings`, not a default.** `true` sends the value to `es_settings.cfg`
  (ES's own store); `false` to SystemConf (`system.cfg`), which is the only place the
  launch scripts read. A row that needs a default-on switch on SystemConf is written by
  hand: `setState(SystemConf::getBool(key, true))` plus an `addSaveFunc` calling
  `setBool`. The PROGRESS TRACKER row passed `true` as a default and its state went
  where no script looks (2026-09-07).
- Lambda capture: `Window* window = mWindow;` then capture `window` (menu may be deleted).
- Wizard page replacement: `cloudSetupPresent(window, current, prev)` closes
  `prev`, and `GuiSettings::close()` ends with `delete this`. Callbacks on the
  new page must hand **that page** to the next transition, not capture the
  deleted predecessor. Both OAuth keyboard choices retained the provider page
  after it was closed and crashed on selection (2026-09-05). The ES repo's
  `python3 tests/cloud-oauth-lifetime.py` checks those transitions with
  AddressSanitizer; it complements, rather than replaces, device UI testing.

## Reusable precedents

- **`GuiBackupStart`/`GuiBackup`** — native backup flow (target-device OptionList →
  busy-anim page → ApiSystem call). Hidden on ROCKNIX (no `ApiSystem::BACKUP` backend);
  the model to follow for a native backuptool page (issue #18 P2+).
- **`GuiFileBrowser`** — directory/file picker; the pattern for the P3 cloud
  directory chooser (feed it rclone `lsf` results).
- **`GuiMoonlight`** — settings+actions hybrid page driving an external tool.
- **`GuiBatoceraStore`/`GuiThemeDownloader`** — list + install with async progress.

## Anti-patterns (observed, avoid)

- **Two surfaces for one event.** A job that reports progress in one shape
  and its outcome in another, somewhere else on screen, changes shape and
  position at exactly the moment somebody is looking for the answer. The
  surface that reported the work says how it ended and then fades — see
  `ThreadedCloudSync::run`. It replaced a card that vanished into a
  `GuiInfoPopup` two hundred pixels away.

- **An operation whose only report is transient.** A progress card and the
  toast that replaces it are both gone within seconds, so anyone who starts a
  job and walks away — which is the normal way to run a backup — returns to a
  screen that has never heard of it. Long-running work must leave a durable
  answer to "did that work?" on the page that offered it: the backend stamps
  the outcome somewhere device-local, and the page reads it back.

  That stamp is necessary and **not sufficient**, which took a second round to
  learn. A row in a menu answers "did the last one work?" for somebody who
  thinks to go and look; it does nothing for somebody standing in front of the
  device when the surface they were watching vanishes. For anything long, the
  durable answer has to be *on the screen that ran it* — see the fourth tier
  above. A log file is not that answer either; nobody is going to be told a
  path.

- Dropping to a fullscreen CLI for things a `GuiSettings` page + headless backend can do
  natively — acceptable as parity stopgap, not as the end state (issue #15 L2).
- Direct `system()`/popen in UI code paths — use `runSystemCommand`/`ApiSystem`/threads.

## Before the pin moves, the compiler has seen the edit

An EmulationStation edit has no compiler nearer than an image build, and a
mistake any compiler catches costs a build cycle to find: on 2026-09-21 a
loop body grew from one statement to three without braces, the pin was
bumped, and GENERIC_X64 run 12 spent twenty minutes to say `'name' was not
declared` (blindspot 49). The build root holds the cross toolchain and
ninja's exact command for every object, so

```bash
tools/es-syntax-check es-app/src/guis/GuiCloudTransfer.cpp   # from the ROCKNIX checkout
```

replays that command on the edited file with `-fsyntax-only` in a few
seconds, PASS or the compiler's errors. It reads headers from the build
tree, so an edit that changes a header is checked with `--with <dir>` or
by the build; it exits 2 when it cannot run, and that is not a pass. An ES
commit that touches a `.cpp` is not ready to merge until this has passed.

# Codebase renovation: the plan for the plan

**Issue:** #346 (M6.P0), under epic #339, milestone M6.
**Decisions:** D-WORKFLOW-083 (the whole codebase, in tiers), D-WORKFLOW-102
(in places, progressively, never one broad sweep; the first item is the
order and the method), D-WORKFLOW-056 (Fable plans to the line, another
model executes), D-WORKFLOW-137 (review depth), D-WORKFLOW-181 (this
widening). Written 2026-10-22 on `feature/m6-renovation-plan-346`.

This document decides **how the renovation of the whole codebase is planned**:
what is surveyed first, how the codebase is cut into slices, how the slices
are ordered, what one slice's work consists of, what a brief for the
executing model must carry, how the program survives feature work landing
beside it, and which ledgers it writes. It does not order the slices; that is
P1's output, `docs/reviews/order.md`, which #346's acceptance criteria name.
It reviews no code.

## 1. What the maintainer asked for

Maintainer, 2026-10-22, quoted as the requirement (D-QA-012):

> "This codebase was a hard fork from ROCKNIX, and that itself was a hard
> fork from a previous operating system. Over the years, I imagine that a
> lot of cruff has built up across the entire sprawl of the operating
> system. Now that we have a new fork, I'd like to have a parallel project
> that runs concurrently with our feature development to do a renovation of
> the codebase."

> "The very first task will be developing a plan for our plan, so that we
> know how we can break this down into increasingly bite-sized chunks."

> "The goal should be for us to develop a way of first surveying the entire
> codebase and understanding it, then breaking it down into a code review
> plan to go top to bottom across the entire codebase and work through it.
> I'd like to make sure that this plan is well defined so that it can be
> handed off in execution to an agent like Opus 5.5, as opposed to relying
> on Fable. I'd like to use Fable to develop all of the plan, the
> milestones, epics, issues, acceptance criteria, etc., and then be able to
> hand it off to a model like Opus 5.5."

> "We also do need to be cognizant of the fact that work will be happening
> in parallel, so there may be times where we need to go back and redo some
> of the review because new functionality may change the codebase. However,
> this should be a relatively small bit of work that needs to be redone
> compared to the sheer scope of the codebase."

> "The goal is to: modernize the codebase; ensure we're adhering to best
> practices, coding standards, and more; identify bugs; look for where
> packages may need to be updated; look for where there's room for
> efficiency in how it works (that's computational, memory management, user
> experience, etc.); find dead ends; make sure the code itself is clear,
> well structured, etc.; in general, try to streamline and improve the
> operating system top to bottom."

How this sits with what was already decided: D-WORKFLOW-083 asked for an
adversarial review of the whole codebase in three tiers; D-WORKFLOW-102
refined it to slices done in places and progressively, under a milestone of
its own, with the first item being the analysis that sets the order and the
method. This request keeps both (the slices still cover the whole, still
progressively, still never as one sweep) and **widens the lens** from finding
defects to renovating: the seven goals above become the seven questions every
slice answers (§ 4). It also fixes the division of labour: Fable writes the
plan, the survey, the order, the epics, the issues and their criteria; a
model such as Opus 5.5 executes a slice from its brief (§ 7), the shape
D-WORKFLOW-056 used for the fix round of 2026-09-28.

Three provenance tiers run through every root, and the tier decides the lens
(§ 4):

- **Fork-own**: written here since the fork (from the merge base with
  `upstream/next` to `next` on the distribution, 126,855 paths of which 125,225
  are records under `docs/`; from the merge base with `rocknix/master` to the
  pin on EmulationStation). A path upstream changed since the merge base and
  the fork never touched is upstream-carried, not fork-own: the two-way diff
  `upstream/next..next` would mislabel 912 of them. About 121,000 lines
  across both (#339). Everything applies: bugs, standards, structure,
  efficiency, dead ends.
- **Upstream-carried**: ROCKNIX's and its upstreams' (JELOS, LibreELEC,
  CoreELEC) code that the image runs. About 140,000 lines of shell and
  recipes (#339). The first questions are different: is it still reached by
  any image we build; is it current with upstream; did upstream fix it since;
  do we carry a local change that upstream has since superseded.
- **Vendor-carried**: patches to third-party sources (kernels, emulators,
  libraries) and kernel configurations. Half a million lines of patches and a
  quarter million of configuration (#339). Never read line by line: one
  provenance row per patch (origin, merged upstream or not, the reason we
  carry it, the version it was made against, whether it still applies), and
  one diff per kernel config against its base.

## 3. Three principles the method rests on

1. **Provenance decides the lens, size decides the slice.** A fork-own file
   gets the full seven questions; an upstream-carried file gets the
   reachability and currency questions first and the rest only if it stays;
   a vendor-carried patch gets a table row. Slices are then cut to a size one
   executing session finishes (§ 5).
2. **A review is a fact about a tree hash.** Every slice issue records the
   paths it covers and the commit it was read at. Drift is then `git diff
   <reviewed-at>..next -- <paths>`: a diff, measurable and small, never a
   re-read (§ 8). This is what makes "work happening in parallel" cost a
   diff and not a slice.
3. **The brief is the unit of handoff.** Fable's output for a slice is a
   brief an executing model can run without this conversation (§ 7). The
   proof that a brief is good enough is the one D-WORKFLOW-133 uses for the
   session stash: a model with no context is given the repository and the
   brief and its first hour is compared with what the brief intended.

## 4. The seven questions a slice answers

The maintainer's goals, each turned into a question with the evidence that
answers it. These are the **renovation face** added to the code-auditor
skill's Phase 3 (§ 6, stage B); the skill's own faces (instruction files,
blindspot register, invariants, cross-system interactions) stay.

| # | Goal | The question the executor answers, per file or unit | Evidence that answers it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Q1 | Modernize | Is this written against an interface, language level, tool or convention that has a current replacement in this tree or upstream (bash idioms the rest of the tree has moved past, `systemd` units written the old way, Python 2 remnants, hand-rolled JSON, a library two majors behind)? | the replacement named with where the tree already uses it; `git log -S` showing when the old form stopped being written |
| Q2 | Standards and best practices | Does it meet the rules in `.claude/rules/` whose `paths:` match it, `packages/README.md` for recipes, and the conventions of its own kind (`set -euo pipefail` and quoting in shell, late binding in `package.mk`, the ES rules for the interface)? | the rule and section cited; `tools/pkgcheck` output for a recipe; `shellcheck` output where it runs |
| Q3 | Bugs | Where does it fail: the unhandled branch, the race, the wrong default, the path that works on the host and not on the device? | a reproduction on the VM or a trace with file:line; the code-auditor evidence floor applies (host reasoning about device behaviour is a lead, not evidence) |
| Q4 | Package currency | Is the pinned version current, and if pinned on purpose does the recipe say why? Does upstream ROCKNIX carry a newer recipe we have not merged? | `tools/fork-package-freshness` for fork-introduced packages; for the rest, the pin against the project's releases with the date checked |
| Q5 | Efficiency | What does it cost at run time: on the launch path (time to play, D-CLOUD-098), at boot, in memory on a 1 GiB handheld, in a loop that runs every exit; and what does it cost the player in steps? | a measurement on the VM (`tools/time-to-play`, `tools/es-launch-memory`, `tools/signin-memory`) or the named absence of one; the player-facing path counted in presses |
| Q6 | Dead ends | Is it reached at all: by any image we build (the device `options`, the package dependency graph), by any caller (`grep` for the symbol, the unit, the script name), by any player path? Is it a half-finished feature, a retired mechanism still carried, a compatibility alias with no retirement condition (NAMING.md)? | the reachability search recorded as a command and its output; `engineering-practices.md` § Before deleting a duplicate applies before any removal |
| Q7 | Clarity and structure | Can a reader new to it tell what it does and why in one pass: naming, one responsibility per unit, no copy of logic that lives elsewhere, comments that match the code, a header that says where it came from? | the specific unit named with what a reader stumbles on; a duplicate named with its original |

A finding is one of the seven with its evidence; the classification is the
code-auditor skill's (severity, category) with `Renovation` added as a
category for Q1, Q5, Q6 and Q7 items that are not defects. Every removal
proposed under Q6 carries the `Already written:` question (D-WORKFLOW-050):
what the retired code left on devices and in clouds, and how the removal
treats it.

## 5. Slicing

**A slice is a set of paths one executing session reviews to a finished
punch list.** Its size is bounded two ways:

- about 8,000 to 12,000 lines of code read line by line, or one package
  group, or one device; #339's packets (about 500 KB a seat) and the fix
  round's briefs (D-WORKFLOW-056) are the precedent for what a session
  finishes;
- the paths that share runtime state stay together, because interaction
  defects live at the seam (code-auditor § Cross-system interaction audit):
  the cloud scripts and the ES pages that call them; `runemu.sh` and the
  emulator wrappers; `backuptool` and the settings archives; the proxy and
  its consumers.

Each slice has one issue, attached as a sub-issue of #339 until its area's
epic is filed at that area's first dispatch (then re-parented, the epic's body
and the title updated with a comment, as `milestone-phase-naming.md` says).
All slices are one declared phase, P2, ordered by `order.md`; the title is
`M6.P2 E339/T<k>: <area>: <slice>` (`T`, verification, from the closed sub-id
set; `k` sequential), becoming `E<epic>/T<k>` under the area epic. It carries: the paths (so `tools/box-check` can read them), the
provenance tier, the line count, the lens questions that apply, the
interacting subsystems, the review depth (§ 6, stage C), the reading
prerequisite if any (the launch-path slices before #336 Step 1; no slice
gates a release, D-WORKFLOW-187), and the `reviewed-at` field left empty
until stage H fills it.

**Areas become epics.** The survey (P1) proposes them; the first cut, from
the shape in § 2, is:

| Epic (area) | Tier | What it holds | Why it is one epic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Build engine | upstream-carried, small fork delta | `scripts/`, `config/`, `distributions/`, the `Makefile`, `tools/mkpkg`, the Docker path | everything else is built by it; 26,000 lines read once; where the maintainer puts the renovation's value, ahead of any device, with the harness and the package currency beside it (D-WORKFLOW-186; #644 reads ROCKNIX's documented build path against ours) |
| OS scripts and launch path | fork-own on upstream | `projects/ROCKNIX/packages/rocknix/` (the OS scripts, `runemu.sh`), `sysutils/` (busybox, systemd units, the quirks), `hardware/` | the launch path is read before #336 Step 1 replaces it (D-WORKFLOW-102 as D-WORKFLOW-187 refines it: a reading order, not a release gate) |
| Cloud sync and saves | fork-own | `projects/ROCKNIX/packages/network/rclone/`, the cloud tools under `tools/`, `backuptool` | one state model, one filter allowlist, the invariants in `rclone-cloud-sync.md` |
| Offline achievements | fork-own | the proxy package, its consumers in RetroArch and the emulators, the ES pages | one protocol, one queue |
| Emulators and cores | upstream-carried with fork patches | `projects/ROCKNIX/packages/emulators/` (276 differing paths), the RetroArch patches, the wrappers | the largest group; split by family (libretro cores, standalone, RetroArch itself) |
| Devices | upstream-carried | `projects/ROCKNIX/devices/*` for the devices we ship (H700 and SM8550; GENERIC_X64 as the test image, D-WORKFLOW-185), their kernels and quirks; every other target is a row | one slice per device we ship; one row per device we do not; RK3566 and RK3326 are the recorded first widening, each a device build with its own issue when the maintainer opens it |
| Generic packages | upstream-carried | `packages/*` by group | reachability first: a group no image we build reaches is a table, not a reading |
| Patches and configs | vendor-carried | every `.patch` under `packages/` and `projects/`, every kernel `.conf` | the provenance table (#339 criterion 2): one row per patch, count equal to `find -name '*.patch' | wc -l` |

A slice an executing session cannot finish is two slices; P1 cuts, the
executor does not re-cut mid-slice (the swarm rule in `ceremonies.md`: a
scope under audit is not mutated from elsewhere, and not re-scoped from
inside).

The milestone body (M6) carries the live order and current/next work
(D-WORKFLOW-139); this is the shape it orders.

### P0, the plan for the plan (this document; #346)

Exit: this document on `next`; D-WORKFLOW-181 in the register; M6's body

their bodies pointing here; the P1 brief written (§ 7) and the P1 issue

### P1, the survey (next; its own issue under #339)

The inventory and the order, produced by the multi-pass
iterative analysis the maintainer uses for collections (seven passes, N-to-N
cross-reference, a tracking file; the copy lives outside the tree, see the
memory `maintainer-meta-process-multi-pass`), at its comprehensive rigour
because this is the first analysis of the scope:

1. **Inventory** (pass 1): `tools/renovation-inventory` walks the tree and
   the ES checkout and writes `docs/reviews/inventory.json`: for every path,
   its root, provenance tier (fork-own is `git diff --name-only $(git merge-base
   upstream/next next) next`; on EmulationStation the merge base with
   `rocknix/master` to the pin; upstream-only changes since the merge base
   are upstream-carried), language, line count, patch count, last fork
   commit, last upstream commit, and reachability (which built images include
   it, from the device `options` and `PKG_DEPENDS_*`). The verification is
   the count: the tool's total equals `git ls-files | wc -l` on both trees,
   and the patch rows equal `find -name '*.patch' | wc -l`.
2. **Clustering** (pass 2): paths into the areas of § 5, written to
   `docs/reviews/inventory.md` with the per-area totals; an area whose read
   size exceeds a session is split here.
3. **Assessment** (pass 3): each area scored on the ordering lenses of § 6a,
   with the evidence for each score (the friction log's and blindspot
   register's entries for brittleness; `git log --since` churn; the open
   issues touching it; the planned changes it is nearest).
4. **Cross-reference** (pass 4): every area against every other for shared
   state and call edges, so the slice boundaries of § 5 are drawn from the
   edges and not from the directory tree.
5. **Classification and reconciliation** (passes 5 and 6): the order, with
   the lens that put each slice where it is, written to
   `docs/reviews/order.md` in the shape #346's first criterion names.
6. **Action** (pass 7): the proposed order and slice list posted on the P1
   issue and the maintainer's yes recorded there (the pattern's pass 7 is
   interactive by its own rule); then the slice issues filed by the
   coordinator lane (D-WORKFLOW-189: the definition of work items is the
   coordinator's; P1's renderer produces the bodies) as sub-issues of
   #339, each with its brief's scope block (area epics are filed lazily at
   each area's first dispatch, so each owes its futro at its own kickoff); the preliminary three-model review of the
   order (`.claude/skills/council/references/review-formats.md`, advisory)
   or the recorded reason it was not run; the register row for the order;

P1's tools, built in P1 because a procedure becomes a tool
(`learning-capture.md` § 3): `tools/renovation-inventory` (above),
`tools/renovation-drift` (§ 8), `tools/renovation-status` (one table: slice,
area, lines, depth, state, reviewed-at, drift since), and the renovation face

### P2 onward, the slices

In the order `order.md` sets, each slice runs the per-slice procedure (§ 6b)
to its resolution gate. Slices in different areas may run in parallel in
their own worktrees; two slices never share a path. A slice's punch list is
resolved in the same cycle (D-WORKFLOW-054: everything found is fixed or
withdrawn with its reason, not only the Critical and High), which is where
the renovation actually happens.

### Standing, drift re-review

Runs at every slice close (§ 8), on the renovation's own cadence and never as
a release step (D-WORKFLOW-187). It is a phase with no end, listed in the
milestone body as such.

### 6a. Ordering lenses

The four the maintainer named in #346, with two the renovation adds. The
survey scores each area on all six and the order is argued from the scores,
not from the directory listing.

| Lens | Puts first | Evidence for the score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Security | code that handles credentials, network input, archives it unpacks, anything that runs as root on a device | the sign-in broker, `rclone.conf` handling, the updater, backup/restore, the proxy's listener |
| Brittleness | the parts that have failed most | entries in `docs/blindspot-register.md` and `docs/friction-log.md` per path; bug issues closed per path; `git log --since=2026-06-01` churn |
| Nearest new functionality | what the fork has changed most since the fork | `git diff --stat $(git merge-base upstream/next next) next` per area; the M7 change log |
| Nearest planned change | what is about to be replaced or extended | #336 (the libretro runner under ES), #576 (GTK4), #509 (the remaining old names), #585 (upstream contributions) |
| Cost against value | small, central, read once | the build engine; the OS scripts; a device we ship |
| Reachability | what no image reaches at all | the inventory's reachability column: unreached code is a dead-end slice reviewed as a table, cheap and early, because removal shrinks every later slice |

The renovation gates no release (D-WORKFLOW-187, refining D-WORKFLOW-102):
a finding that is a defect is a bug issue and holds or clears a release the
way every bug does (D-QA-051). One reading order stands regardless of the
scores: the OS launch, control and state slice and the interface's launch-path
slice are read before #336 Step 1 replaces what they read.

`tools/lint-audit-artifacts` runs before stage D and again before stage H;
the renovation face is added to its checks in P1 so a slice without the seven
questions answered fails the lint rather than a reader's attention.

**The stream practice (added 2026-10-26 from T17's second hand-back, #664).**
A stage-E stream that changes a script `tools/last-good-scripts-test` covers
runs that suite before its commit and names the run in `02` § The streams;
a stream that changes an EmulationStation source runs the unit tests and
the syntax check the slice's brief names, or records their `CANNOT`. T17's
S3 narrowed a check too far and the suite found it only at S7
(`c3e260861b` put it right); the suite before the commit would have found
it at S3. And a suite that asserts the defect the stream fixes changes in

suite passing after with its count named (D-WORKFLOW-210: T29's S3 for

stand-in absent where the image always has one -- is completed in the same

and the better shape rewrites nothing -- the real script in an unprivileged

environment (`bwrap --clearenv`), since #549's lesson about `TMPDIR` holds at
every execution boundary, not only Docker's. Every stream brief carries
those two lines when a fixture is in its plan.

**The brief practice that grew in P2 (added 2026-10-26 from the coordinator's
retro, `docs/retros/2026-10-26-m6-coordinator.md`).** Before any dispatch: a
**stranger's proof** -- a reader with no context, at most ten commands, from a
scratch clone, runs the brief's membership block and its runs block and
spot-checks every figure and line number; **version 2** of the brief records
each correction in a list at its end, and the futro's kickoff addendum takes
an errata section. In the brief itself: **every figure names its population**
(the slice's paths, the directory, the tree), **every block is runnable from a
clone** (path-safe forms: `-z`, `xargs -0`, Python over `ls-tree -r -z`; never
`awk '{print $4}'` or `$(cat paths)` over paths that may carry spaces),
**every binary or path is named only after `ls` has seen it**, and a claim
about a writer or a caller comes from the grep that finds the write, not from
a verb's name in a comment. At acceptance the lane's deltas become an **errata
section** appended to the brief, never edited into its sections: the brief is
the record of what was asked. Every version-1 brief of P2 needed its proof
(twelve to seventeen corrections each), and twice the proof refuted the
premise the lens was built on. A claim about another repository's table -- a `whySentences` row, a
catalog's entry, a menu map's line -- names the read that shows it at that
repository's pin, as the membership block does for this one; T17's S6 was
briefed on a row the table did not hold (#1133's criterion was reworded). A count a brief states is produced by the binary a script will get --
`/usr/bin/grep`, `command grep` -- never the interactive shell's `grep`, which
here is a ugrep function with a different dialect: T18's declaration count
read 47 there and 44 under GNU `grep -E`, which takes `\s` inside `[...]`
literally (#1138). The stranger's proof runs from a script for the same
reason.

### 6c. Review depth per slice

From the code-auditor review levels (D-WORKFLOW-137), chosen in P1 and
recorded on the slice issue before dispatch:

| Slice | Depth |
| --- | --- |
| a dead-end table, a provenance table, a doctrine read | Local: the executor alone; the lint and the counts are the check |
| an ordinary code slice | Independent: the executor plus one reviewer from another lab |
| a security, state-preservation or launch-path slice; the cloud sync; the updater | Extended: two reviewers from two other labs |

The executor is an Anthropic model, so the reviewer is not: GPT-6 Astra
(`--member gpt --provider openrouter`, `max`) is the default second lab, and
Gemini 4 Argon, verified operational on #638/#639, is the third for extended
depth. Fable cannot be a reviewer of Opus's work under this rule: same lab.
The five-seat council is not a slice's reviewer; it is the escalation a
release may be assigned (`adversarial-council.md`). The preliminary review of
the order in P1 is a different thing again: its three seats (Claude, Gemini,
GPT) are fixed by the format's own contract
(`.claude/skills/council/references/review-formats.md`) and it is advisory,
so the lab exclusion above does not apply to it, and a seat that fails
verification is recorded, never substituted.

## 7. The brief: what the executor receives

A brief is a Markdown file under `docs/reviews/briefs/<slice>.md`, written
by the planner and committed before dispatch, that an executing session runs
start to finish without this conversation. Its sections, in order, each
mandatory:

1. **Identity**: the slice issue, the epic, the milestone phase, the branch
   and worktree (`feature/m6-<slice>-<issue>` under
   `/workspace/repos/pixelelated/distribution.worktrees/m6-<slice>-<issue>`,
   the issue number appended, as T1 #648 and T2 #649 do; an interface
   slice adds an EmulationStation worktree
   `emulationstation-next.worktrees/m6-<slice>-<issue>` on
   `feature/m6-<slice>-<issue>` from the pin), the model
   and effort the maintainer selected, the review depth and reviewer
   recipes.
2. **Scope**: the paths, the tree hash they are read at, the line count per
   path (the executor re-counts; a count that differs is recorded as a delta
   beside the brief's, and the stop is a hash that is not the one named, a
   count that cannot be produced, or two commands for one quantity that
   disagree), the provenance tier, the interacting subsystems and their paths (read-only
   context).
3. **Read first**: the rule files in scope by name, read from `next`; the
   blindspot entries that touch these paths by number; the prior audits of
   these paths under `docs/audits/` (as provenance; the skill has no Phase 2.5 at
   epic tier, so the verdicts are read after the slice's own Phase 2 is
   written, compared then, and never transcribed into it); the decisions by ID that settle questions the slice
   might otherwise re-open.
4. **The questions**: § 4's table restated for this slice, with the questions
   that do not apply struck and the reason (a provenance table has no Q5).
5. **The evidence floor**: the code-auditor's rules as its SKILL.md § Evidence
   floor lists them; what runs on the VM and how (`generic-x64-vm-testing.md`
   § headless), with every tool the brief names run with `--help` and every
   host path it names listed before the brief is committed (the first
   slice brief had six such claims wrong, futro 2026-10-23); what never
   runs (no device, no cloud, no build in a build worktree, no edit to a tool
   that is in flight, no `pkill -f`).
6. **Outputs**: the audit folder name, the six phase files, the YAML index,
   the audit issue's title shape, the retro's path, the fields to fill on the
   slice issue at close.
7. **Acceptance**: the slice issue's checklist, every item agent-verifiable
   (D-QA-044): the lint's PASS line, the counts, the issue's checkboxes, the
   `reviewed-at` hash present.
8. **Stop conditions**: completion; an explicit maintainer pause; a blocker
   named with what is needed; a hash mismatch at stage A (a differing count
   is a delta, not a stop). A checkpoint is not a stop (D-WORKFLOW-149). Nothing else ends the session
   early, and an idle session reports itself idle.
9. **Ceremonies owed**: the work-log entry per session, headed by the issue;
   `tools/work-log-index --write`; a friction line the moment something
   slows; the retro at close; the register row for any decision the slice
   forces; the ceremony check before the push.
10. **Hand-back**: what the planner reads to accept the slice: the audit
    issue's checkboxes all ticked with their outcomes, the lint PASS, the
    status table's row, the retro's four answers.

**The planner keeps** the order, the cutting, the briefs, the acceptance of
a slice against its brief, the register, and the milestone body. The planner
does not re-review a slice the executor finished; it reads the artifacts the
brief named and runs the lint. A brief that needed the planner's help
mid-slice is a defect in the brief, logged as friction and fixed in the brief
template here.

## 8. Parallel work and drift

Feature work (M7 and after) lands on `next` while slices run. The rules:

- **Every slice records its hash.** Stage A reads at a commit; stage H writes
  `reviewed-at: <hash>` and `fixed-at: <hash>` on the slice issue and in the
  inventory. A review is a fact about that tree.
- **Drift is a diff, found by a tool.** `tools/renovation-drift` (built in
  P1) lists, for every closed slice, `git diff --stat <fixed-at>..next --
  <paths>`: files touched, lines changed, and whether any touched file is on
  the security, state-preservation or launch-path list. It runs at every
  slice close, on the renovation's own cadence and not as a release step
  (D-WORKFLOW-187).
- **A small drift is re-reviewed at issue tier.** Under 20 % of the slice's
  lines and no listed file: a local, issue-tier pass over the diff only, by
  the executor, with its own short audit folder (`issue-<slice>-drift-<date>`)
  and no second opinion. The slice's `reviewed-at` moves forward.
- **A large drift re-opens the slice** at its original depth over the diff
  and the files the diff touches, not the whole slice. Over 20 %, or any
  listed file touched, or an interacting subsystem replaced (the libretro
  runner replacing the RetroArch launch path is the known case).
- **The swarm rule holds in both directions.** A slice issue says which
  paths are under review and from when; a feature branch that must touch
  them either waits for stage H or announces itself on the slice issue, and
  the slice re-baselines at stage A on the merged tree rather than reading a
  moving one (code-auditor § Execution discipline). Slices are cut to days,
  not weeks, so this costs little.
- **Two lanes, one tree.** Slice worktrees are cut from `next` and merged to
  `next`; they never merge another lane's feature history to refresh rules
  (`session-resume`, D-WORKFLOW-140). Where two lanes append to the same
  ledger (the register, a day's work log, the index), the merge keeps both
  appends and regenerates the index; neither lane edits the other's rows.
- **One coordinator lane, one session per worktree** (D-WORKFLOW-183,
  2026-10-22). `feature/m6-renovation-plan-346` is the program's coordinator
  lane, as `m7-player-setup` is M7's: it plans, writes briefs, accepts at
  gates and integrates. Each executing phase or slice is one worktree with
  one session; a second session never shares a checkout (one index per
  worktree, the 2026-09-14 mixed-image failure), and fan-out inside a lane is
  read-only research subagents whose leads the lane re-derives. There is no
  long-lived M6 integration branch: `next` is the roll-up, because
  remediation must be built and VM-tested there; a slice stacks on the P1
  chain only while `next` is gated, and merges in order afterwards.
- **The canonical stash is one file with two writers**, which the M7 lane
  and this lane will both reach for. Until the maintainer settles it, this
  lane keeps its state in its branch pointer
  (`.github/sessions/saved-session-state-feature-m6-renovation-plan-346.md`)
  and does not edit `saved-session-state-next.md` while M7 owns it; the
  question is recorded on #346.

# EmulationStation UI style guide

How a screen should look and behave, derived from what this codebase already
does — not invented. Every rule below is backed by shipped code; where the tree
is inconsistent, that is said plainly rather than papered over.

**This was `docs/es-ui-style-guide.md` until 2026-09-12**, where nothing loaded
it. Maintainer, #147: *"I think it makes sense to make the style guide into an
instruction rules file so we don't lose it."* (D-WORKFLOW-007.)

Companion: [es-menu-map.md](../../docs/es-menu-map.md) — where a new screen
belongs. Deeper background: `es-native-ui.md` (the building blocks),
`es-player-text.md` (the words), `es-code-traps.md` (the sharp edges).

Upstream documents **none** of this: `THEMES.md` covers only repainting menus.
The Batocera wiki contributes the interaction rules in the last section.

The project name **pixelelated** always stays lowercase, including labels and
headings otherwise written in capitals (D-WORKFLOW-144). Do not uppercase the
brand through a component formatter.

## Keep the flow and its visual evidence together

**Required for every EmulationStation change, and for any navigation,
information-architecture, behavior or screen-content change regardless of
which repository or script supplies it** (D-UI-039, D-WORKFLOW-155/156):

1. Review the affected canonical menu map and flow/IA diagram. Update the
   steps, labels, branch triggers and destinations with the implementation.
   A text-only change still updates its screen/flow reference. Inventory
   distinct content variants (including each category's help and displayed
   script warnings) plus rejected/error states before declaring coverage
   complete. One shared page/component does not prove all of its copy variants.
2. Capture the accompanying screenshots from the changed source on the VM;
   review the happy path and relevant branches, including cancellation,
   failure/retry and stale state where applicable. For a change with no
   intended visible effect, name the exercised flow and retain the screenshot
   proving its unchanged presentation; do not invent diagram changes.
3. Link each reviewed frame to its flow step/branch and exact source or build,
   language, panel size and expected state. Record any reused evidence with
   its original source and an explicit unchanged-input justification. A
   missing or rejected proof remains open; it cannot satisfy completion.
4. Land source, canonical references and evidence together before calling the
   UI change complete or promoting its product pin. Keep a machine-readable
   evidence index beside the reviewed frames, following the format in the
   menu map. This applies during fixes as well as initial implementation.

A directory of unnamed screenshots is not a flow reference. The current
`es-menu-map-check` detects missing screen titles, not stale copy or screenshot
coverage; passing it alone does not satisfy these required steps.

Use the existing `vm-walks`, `vm-visual-qa` and `frame-diff` mechanisms.
Draft source-overlay frames do not replace the accepted device baseline.
Retain the previous evidence as historical and record intentional differences
with their owning issue; never silently bless a changed screen by replacing
its reference. The menu map's visual-evidence section is the entrypoint.

## Rows

Seven builders. Pick by what the row *is*, not by how it looks.

| Row | Builder | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| Action | `addEntry(label, arrow, func)` | do something / go somewhere |
| Setting | `addWithLabel(label, component)` | a value the player changes |
| Either + explanation | `addWithDescription(label, desc, comp_or_null, func)` | when one line of "what does this do" is needed |
| Section header | `addGroup(label)` | segment a page |
| Text / password | `addInputTextConfigRow(label, key, password)` | free text bound to a config key |
| Read-only fact | `addWithLabel(label, TextComponent)` | a value the player reads, not edits |
| Raw | `addRow(ComponentListRow)` | only when the helpers cannot express it |

The mechanical difference: an **action** row has a `func` and no component;
a **setting** row attaches a component on the right and lets it consume
left/right. `addWithDescription` supports both.

Controls: `SwitchComponent` for binary, `OptionListComponent` for 2+ exclusive
values (or multi-select), `SliderComponent` for a continuum. Sliders render
`value+suffix` with no space — `%`, `m`, `s`, `Mb`.

### The `multiLine` trap

Descriptions are **always visible** in both modes — `multiLine` controls
*wrapping*, not visibility:

- `multiLine = true` → the description wraps and the row grows taller.
- `multiLine = false` → the description is clamped to one line and marquee-scrolls
  only while the row is focused. It also forces the whole list into per-frame
  updates.

Which you get is decided by **which overload you hit**, and the two disagree:

```cpp
s->addWithDescription(label, desc, comp);          // multiLine = true  → wraps
s->addWithDescription(label, desc, nullptr, func); // multiLine = false → marquee
```

So a *setting* row with a description wraps, while an *action* row with a
description does not. If an action row needs a wrapped explanation, pass
`multiLine = true` explicitly, or emit one non-selectable small-font row per
line (the wizard's `cloudSetupAddInfoRow`).

### Size by weight, not by helper

Three sizes, and which one a row gets is decided by what the row *is*:

| Size | Used for |
|---|---|
| group font | section headers (`addGroup`) |
| **text font** | row content — actions, statuses, instructions, facts, commands |
| small font | a row's *description*, explaining the row above it |

Peer items must match. A status line sitting beside an action row is the same
weight as that action and takes the same size; only text that explains another
row drops to small. `MultiLineMenuEntry` already draws its substring small, so
descriptions get this for free.

The failure to watch for is size chosen by *plumbing* rather than by weight — a
row rendering small because it happened to go through a helper that reached for
the small font. That shipped once: the cloud wizard drew "SSH SERVICE IS
ENABLED" a size below the action directly above it, and rendered the ssh command
— the most important thing on its page — smaller than the facts beneath it.

### Dim, don't hide

When a feature exists but is not yet configured, keep its rows visible and
dimmed — alpha `0x50` via `(color & 0xFFFFFF00) | 0x50` — and make them offer
the setup flow. Hiding them tells the player nothing; dimming shows what they'd
get. **Dimmed rows must still carry their description**: before setup is exactly
when someone is deciding whether the feature is worth configuring.

## Text

**Write every user-visible string already upper-cased in the source.** The
component only upper-cases four of eleven cases — notably `addEntry` labels,
`addGroup` labels and subtitles are *not* upper-cased for you.

Descriptions are the exception, and the tree has two dialects: upstream Batocera
uses sentence case ("Reduces power consumption when idle."), fork code uses ALL
CAPS. **Match the fork dialect in fork code**; one sentence, ending in a period,
`X: Y` for direction or scope, naming the concrete consequence:

> `GAME SAVES, SAVE STATES, AND SCREENSHOTS: DEVICE TO CLOUD.`
> `RESTORE SETTINGS FIRST, THEN RESTART?`

The first example carried `SAVESTATES AND SCREENSHOTS` until the #147 sweep:
one word where the rule says two, and no serial comma. The shipped strings
were already right (`GuiMenu.cpp:4450`, `:4804`, `:5433`); the style guide's
model was not, which is the worse way round. *Save state* is two words and
the last item of a list keeps its comma (`es-player-text.md` § Conventions,
D-UI-022/048). The second example read `RESTORE SYSTEM SETTINGS FIRST` until
#148 dropped the word *system*: the tier is **settings** (D-UI-022), and
*system settings* named a tier that does not exist.

Placeholders: `AUTO` for "system decides", `NONE` for explicitly nothing,
`<NOT SET>` for a missing credential. Passwords display as `*********`, never
the real value. Button *help* text is lower case, contrasting with its
UPPER-CASE label (`addButton(_("CONTINUE"), _("continue"), …)`).

## Confirmations

The shape, with **YES first** — there is no counter-example in the tree:

```cpp
new GuiMsgBox(window, MESSAGE_ENDING_IN_QUESTION, _("YES"), doIt, _("NO"), nullptr)
```

Safety comes from the back-button accelerator, which binds to a button named
exactly `NO` or `OK` — **and falls through to the last button if neither
exists**. Never let "back" land on the destructive choice. Ending the message
with `?` also selects the question icon automatically.

Escalate wording with severity:

1. **Reversible** — `ARE YOU SURE?`
2. **Consequential** — consequence paragraph, blank line, then the question.
   Reassure explicitly when the action sounds worse than it is:
   `SYNC GAME SAVES BOTH WAYS?\n\nTHE NEWEST COPY OF EACH SAVE IS KEPT ON BOTH SIDES. NOTHING IS DELETED.`
3. **Irreversible** — `WARNING:` prefix, `!`-terminated clauses, and a closing
   question that **restates the verb** (`RESET SYSTEM AND RESTART?`), never a
   generic "continue?".

A failed precondition uses a single-OK box and returns early — but if the
precondition is *fixable*, offer the fix instead of just refusing
(`NO CLOUD REMOTE IS CONFIGURED YET.\n\nSET UP YOUR CLOUD REMOTE NOW?`).
"Already running" is phrased as an offer to stop, not an error.

## Waiting

| Mechanism | Use when |
|---|---|
| `GuiLoading<T>` | seconds; the player must wait; result drives the next screen |
| `AsyncNotificationComponent` | seconds, for fast work the player keeps using the UI through (a two-second save sync, a Bluetooth scan); anything measured in minutes is a fourth-tier page with CANCEL, D-UI-078 (this row said "minutes" until 2026-10-27, a reversal-sweep miss found by T34's research) |
| `displayNotificationMessage` | it finished; nothing to decide |
| `BusyComponent` member | a bespoke screen with its own lifecycle |

Only put genuinely slow work behind a spinner. Fast local calls should run
synchronously — a spinner that flashes for 100 ms is worse than none. Toast
shape is `<glyph> <subject> : <outcome>`.

## Saving

**`addSaveFunc` (apply-on-close) is the default** — batched, and both stores are
written once. Use `setOnChangedCallback` (immediate) only when: a service must
start/stop now, the page must rebuild because the toggle reveals other rows, or
the value must survive ES being killed. Immediate callbacks must persist
themselves.

Guard destructive writes: apply a credential only when it is non-empty *and*
changed, so opening an editor and backing out cannot clear it.

## Reboot-required

Two flags on the page: `"reboot"` (notify) and `"exitreboot"` (notify, and quit
if the user opted in). Set inside `addSaveFunc`, gated on the setter actually
reporting a change; consume in `onFinalize`. A child page sets the flag on its
**parent**, which owns the message. The exact toast is
`_U("\uF011  ") + _("REBOOT REQUIRED TO APPLY THE NEW CONFIGURATION")`.

Settings whose effect is deferred may also say so in their description
("A reboot may be required for changes to take full effect.").

## Buttons

`BACK` is added automatically and is **always last**; anything else precedes it
in decreasing prominence. For a wizard, `clearButtons()` and replace the row:
exit on the left, advance on the right.

**Gate by existence, not by disabling.** Pass a null callback and the button is
not built — so CONTINUE literally does not exist until it would work:

```cpp
s->getMenu().clearButtons();
s->getMenu().addButton(_("EXIT SETUP"), _("exit setup"), [s] { s->close(); });
if (onContinue != nullptr)
    s->getMenu().addButton(_("CONTINUE"), _("continue"), onContinue);
```

A page the player may defer offers `LATER` (left) and `FINISH` (right), where
only FINISH consumes any one-shot marker.

## Glyphs

The status pair is the most reusable convention in the codebase:

| Glyph | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `\uF058` check-circle | done / verified / present |
| `\uF071` exclamation-triangle | needs attention |

Prefix a **row label** with two trailing spaces (`_U("\uF058  ")`), a
**notification** with one. When a state needs no action, put the glyph on a
non-selectable row instead of an actionable one.

Named theme icons (`iconGames`, `iconNetwork`, …) are used **only on the
top-level main menu** — no sub-page passes one, and the vocabulary is fixed, so
sub-pages use glyph prefixes.

## Gating

Four gates, in order of precedence:

1. `ApiSystem::isScriptingSupported(FEATURE)` — backend script present.
2. `Utils::FileSystem::exists(...)` — our own tooling. Nest it: feature exists →
   feature configured → individual sub-tool.
3. Kid / kiosk mode — anything that runs shell commands, resets state or edits
   credentials sits behind `isFullUI`.
4. Runtime preconditions — checked at entry with an early return, not at build.

Show a row only when it is meaningful: an account row appears because a username
survived the backup; a netplay row because netplay is on. Expensive checks
(network round-trips) belong behind an explicit user action, never at page build.

## Wizards

- **Push the new page, then close the old one.** Closing first flashes the menu
  underneath. Never call `close()` on the page that owns the running handler and
  then touch its captures — that is a use-after-free.
- **Title stays constant; the step goes in the subtitle** (`STEP 1 OF 3 - SET UP SSH`),
  separated by a spaced hyphen. Subtitles are not auto-upper-cased.
- **Rebuild the page after an edit** so every row re-reads live state.
- **`LOG(LogInfo)` at every state transition**, prefixed with the flow name.
- **Only build a gated wizard when a real sequence exists.** If the items are
  independent and optional, one page of verified rows is correct — a forced
  sequence for optional work is worse than a list.

## Interaction rules (from upstream)

- Refer to buttons by **cardinal position** (North/South/East/West), never
  console letters — labels differ per controller.
- **South confirms, East cancels** by default, and the player can swap them, so
  never hardcode "press A".
- **START** opens the main menu anywhere; **SELECT** opens the context menu.
- Provide `getHelpPrompts()` so the bottom help bar stays accurate — upstream
  states the help bar is how players learn the current assignments.

## Known inconsistencies

Documented so nobody "fixes" one half into the other by accident:

- The arrow flag on action rows is applied inconsistently — the QUIT menu passes
  `false` for rows that open confirm boxes, the reset menu passes `true`.
- `MenuComponent::addEntry` and `GuiSettings::addEntry` **swap parameters 5 and
  6** (`setCursorHere` / `onButtonRelease`). Both are `bool`, so a mix-up
  compiles silently.
- Two description dialects (sentence case upstream, ALL CAPS in fork code).

## 1. What do we know and what are we assuming?

questions), at Extended depth (Astra and Argon through the Facilitator),

of 2026-10-23 (which carries the pin), pauses at stage D for the
coordinator's stream briefs, fixes on its ES branch with the unit tests and
a syntax-only compile as the compile-side floor, and hands back with three
hashes (`reviewed-at:`, `fixed-at:`, `fixed-at-es:`). The coordinator
accepts, merges the ES branch into `test/qa-integration`, bumps the pin,

## 2. What known unknowns need investigation?

1. **When the host comes back.** M7's reclaim and bounded compile and VM
   work have no stated length. *Proceeding:* the brief makes the return
   line a wait, not a stop; stage A's reading, the counts and the four
   host checks need no runtime; Phases 1 to 4 can be written from the tree
   with the guest proofs held in a list and run when the line comes. The
   coordinator relays the line on #649 and #648.
2. **Whether `es-syntax-check` is fixed before stage E** (#699). *Decided
   here:* the lane fixes it at stage A on its distribution branch as the
   first `bug` it needs (lanes fix bugs; the fix is to the tool's command
   string, never to a build root's wrapper files, which are M7's frozen
   builds), and uses the brief's recipe until then.
3. **Which image proves an ES fix, and when.** M6 builds nothing
   (D-WORKFLOW-183); an ES fix has no binary until a pin bump reaches an
   image, and the M7 lane builds on its own cadence for its own candidate.
   The plan's stage F says every behaviour claim is proven on the VM, and
   its stage H closes at hand-back. For an interface slice the two cannot
   both be true on the day of hand-back. *Decided here, the coordinator's
   call (plan § 6b stage H is amended in the same change):* an interface
   slice is accepted at hand-back and its branches merged and the pin
   bumped, but it is closed only when the first image carrying the new pin
   proves each fix (`renovation-status` lists it as `remediating` until
   then, with `fixed-at-es:` set). Which build carries the renovation's pin
   bumps, M7's next or one the coordinator asks the maintainer for, is put
   to the maintainer on #346 and recorded as an open decision; nothing in
   T2 waits on the answer before its hand-back.
4. **Whether any player runs a custom `es_systems_custom.cfg` that uses
   the raw placeholders.** Not knowable from the tree. *Proceeding:* the
   raw substitutions are Q6 rows on the image (the shipped template uses
   `%RUNCOMMAND%` and `%ROM%` only) and Q3 leads under a custom template,
   which the VM can exercise with a template under `/storage`; a `bug` for
   one is filed with that fixture as its VM criterion, and its severity is
   graded against the custom-template precondition, not as a default path.
5. **Whether T1's punch list and T2's overlap at the command's seam.** T1
   found F-14 (a typed netplay host reaches `runemu.sh`'s root `eval`);
   the ES side `shellQuote`s the ip and nick under `#if ROCKNIX` and the
   shell unquotes them before `runemu.sh` evals. *Proceeding:* the brief
   tells the lane to read T1's audit issue before filing a `bug` on the
   command's quoting; the coordinator writes the two lanes' stream briefs
   for that seam together at the pauses.

## 3. What patterns from prior work apply that we haven't named?

- **T1's brief went out with seven wrong claims and nineteen unasked
  questions; the stranger's proof found them in an hour.** Every one was
  a fact a command could check. So this brief was written after the
  commands: every tool's `--help`, the four host checks run at the pin,
  the unit tests built, the syntax recipe proven, the remote and hooks
  probed, the seam map re-derived line by line. The proof runs again on
  version 1 anyway; what it finds is what the commands did not reach.

"""T44 immutable input binding. Reads Git objects; writes metadata, never sources.

Selector grammar independently reproduced by P1's retained derive.py. This
reader does not execute renovation-inventory, a recipe, or an accepted test.
